mss-c60efd5db6f5ec7808b4.text: In {{c2::chronic kidney disease (CKD)}}, the combination of elevated PTH and decreased 1,25-(OH)2D3 causes {{c1::renal osteodystrophy::pathology}}, in which there is increased bone resorption and osteomalacia
mss-c60efd5db6f5ec7808b4.extra:
- Due to secondary hyperparathyroidism, patient presents with bone pain, painful nodules / skin necrosis (due to tissue calcifications), electrolyte abnormalities

- If left untreated / develops further, constant stimulation of parathyroid leads to tertiary hyperparathyroidism (osteitis fibrosa cystica — bone pain and fractures due to bone cysts and brown tumors)

- Patients have hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and a failure to hydroxylate vitamin D, leading to a secondary hyperparathyroidism

mss-843ab6a8c2a4b5824236.text: {{c1::Hypophosphatemic rickets}} is an inherited disorder resulting in increased {{c2::phosphate}} wasting at the {{c2::proximal tubule}}; results in rickets-like presentation
mss-843ab6a8c2a4b5824236.extra:
- In contrast to vitamin D-dependent rickets, the only lab abnormality is hypophosphatemia (normal Ca2+, vitamin D, and PTH)

- X-linked dominant inheritance

- Can be treated with burosumab (anti-FGF23); osteocytes normally secrete FGF23 in response to elevated calcitriol, which then suppresses both Na+-phosphate cotransport in proximal tubule and suppresses 1α-hydroxylase

mss-bc32bd5f30c1dbfbcd21.text:
What is the treatment for a patient with giant cell arteritis (GCA)?

{{c1::High-dose glucocorticoids}} ± {{c1::tocilizumab*}}
mss-bc32bd5f30c1dbfbcd21.extra:
*Give patients with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis with an increased risk of glucocorticoid-related adverse effects tocilizumab or methotrexate as part of a glucocorticoid-sparing therapy

- Initiate treatment with high-dose glucocorticoid therapy immediately (before the biopsy results return)

- Production of IL-6 is highly associated with severity of the disease, thus tocilizumab can be used to treat GCA (temporal arteritis)

- Patients with an increased risk of glucocorticoid-related side effects: osteoporosis, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, or glaucoma

mss-476765e9c683cede7490.text: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a necrotizing vasculitis that involves most organs, except the {{c1::lungs}}
mss-476765e9c683cede7490.extra:
- Commonly involves the renal and visceral vessels (thus often involving the kidney, heart, GI tract, and liver)

Other clinical features:
- Renal (~ 60%): HTN, renal impairment
- Coronary artery (~ 35%): ↑ risk of MI
- Skin (~ 40%): rash, ulcerations, nodules
- GI: abdominal pain, melena, nausea, vomiting
- Neuro: polyneuropathy, stroke

mss-30c628b23d79a76212c7.text: Patients with Kawasaki disease may develop coronary artery {{c1::aneurysms}}, which can rupture; therefore, get a(n) {{c1::echocardiogram::diagnostic test}}
mss-30c628b23d79a76212c7.extra:
- Perform echocardiography at the time of diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6 - 8 weeks later

- Dilated arteries are prone to thrombotic occlusion, which may cause myocardial ischemia and/or infarction

Risk for aneurysm increases with:
- Age < 1 or > 9 years
- Delay of treatment > 10 days or failure of IVIG treatment
- Recurrence of fever after 2 weeks

mss-669cf111a3a326b950fb.text:
The symptoms of {{c1::Kawasaki}} disease may be remembered with the mnemonic "CRASH and Burn":

{{c1::Conjunctivitis (bilateral)::C}}
{{c1::Rash (polymorphous → desquamating)::R}}
{{c1::Adenopathy (unilateral; cervical lymph nodes)::A}}
{{c1::Strawberry tongue (oral mucositis)::S}}
{{c1::Hand-foot erythema and edema::H}}
&
{{c1::Fever ≥ 5 days::Burn}}
mss-669cf111a3a326b950fb.extra:
- Kawasaki disease criteria: fever ≥ 5 days with ≥ 4 of the CRASH symptoms above

- Classic manifestations typically include labs indicative of systemic inflammation (i.e., thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, and sterile pyuria)




Photo credit: Dong Soo Kim, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mss-eb42992a9319c9a74205.text: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a segmenting {{c1::medium}}-vessel vasculitis that extends into contiguous {{c2::veins}} and {{c2::nerves}}
mss-eb42992a9319c9a74205.extra:
- Buerger disease is also known as thromboangiitis obliterans
- Extension into veins and nerves is rarely seen in other types of vasculitis; commonly involves the tibial and radial arteries
- This relatively spares the vessel wall (intact internal elastic lamina)

mss-522534331eb5af7d9588.text:
Which vasculitis is characterized by a triad of:

1) Focal necrotizing vasculitis
2) Necrotizing granulomas in the lung and upper airway
3) Necrotizing glomerulonephritis

{{c1::Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)}}
mss-522534331eb5af7d9588.extra:
- Upper tract → sinusitis / otitis, blood
- Lower tract → nodules / cavitation / ulceration, blood
- Renal → ↑ Cr, rapidly crescentric GN, blood
- Skin → leukocytoclastic vasculitis, pyoderma gangrenosum (see above); due to impaired healing from vasculitis-induced blood vessel damage → ischemia / necrosis

- GPA was formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis






Photo credit: See page for author, CC BY 4.0 (photo 1) & Crohnie, Public domain (photo 2), both via Wikimedia Commons

mss-6fdcd0a0ffa0fec35507.text:
The classic clinical triad of {{c2::IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)}} is:

{{c1::Palpable purpura}} on the buttocks and legs
{{c1::Arthralgias}}
{{c1::Abdominal}} pain
mss-6fdcd0a0ffa0fec35507.extra:
- Abdominal pain is due to intussusception
- Hematuria is from IgA nephropathy

- UWorld: in addition to the classic symptoms, up to 1/3 of boys with IgA vasculitis have unilateral or bilateral scrotal pain and swelling

- In children with the classic findings, no additional diagnostic testing is needed
- In children with an atypical presentation (or adults), the next step is a skin biopsy

mss-7a5ab697a32c8ccb5a81.text: {{c1::IgA nephropathy (Berger disease)}} is a renal pathology with similar pathophysiology to IgA-vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)
mss-7a5ab697a32c8ccb5a81.extra:
The renal manifestations of IgA vasculitis are indistinguishable from IgA nephropathy; however, they are distinct diseases:
- IgA nephropathy is common in adults and is limited to the kidneys
- IgA vasculitis is common in children and affects multiple organs (joints, hematological, GIT)

- Order urinalysis when IgA vasculitis is diagnosed

- This card used to say that IgA nephropathy is associated with IgA vasculitis but AMBOSS confirms that they are separate diseases with similar pathophysiology (Aug 2025)

mss-248365c0f1bdbd436ed6.text:
The consequences of {{c1::renal failure}} may be remembered with the mnemonic "MAD HUNGER":

{{c1::Metabolic Acidosis::M.A}}
{{c1::Dyslipidemia::D}} (especially increased {{c1::triglycerides}})
{{c1::Hyperkalemia::H}}
{{c1::Uremia::U}}
{{c1::Na+ / H2O retention::N}}
{{c1::Growth retardation and developmental delay::G}}
{{c1::Erythropoietin deficiency (anemia)::E}}
{{c1::Renal osteodystrophy::R}}
mss-248365c0f1bdbd436ed6.extra:
- Metabolic Acidosis: failure of the glomerulus to filter out organic acids leads to an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis if damage to both glomeruli and tubules; if renal damage predominantly affects tubule, normal anion gap

- Dyslipidemia: protein loss in urine due to faulty glomerulus stimulates liver synthesis (additionally, impaired clearance of chylomicrons and VLDL)

- Hyperkalemia: not able excrete potassium

- Uremia: nausea, lethargy, anorexia, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction (urate inhibits platelet adhesion / aggregation), asterixis (flapping hand tremor, urate disrupts function of diencephalic motor centers)

- Na+ / H2O retention: Na+ / H2O retention leads to hypertension; amount of water retention ranges from mild edema to life threatening pulmonary edema

- Erythropoietin failure (anemia): decreased erythropoietin production by renal peritubular interstitial fibroblasts results in normocytic, nonhemolytic anemia

- Renal osteodystrophy: hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism, bone pain, electrolyte abnormalities, tissue calcifications (painful nodules / skin necrosis)

How do levels of parathyroid hormone change in chronic kidney disease?

- Decreased phosphate excretion → hyperphosphatemia → increased release of PTH

mss-3e1b694b7866ea919009.text:
What musculoskeletal disorder is characterized by metaplasia of skeletal muscle to bone?

{{c1::Myositis ossificans}}
mss-3e1b694b7866ea919009.extra:
- Can occur in the setting of trauma to the muscle (non-hereditary form / myositis ossificans traumatica)

- Can also be inherited, autosomal dominant (myositis ossificans progressiva): mutation in the activin type 1 receptor causes endothelial cells to transform to mesenchymal cells and then to bone

- Unlike osteosarcoma, myositis ossificans is separated from the bone and is present in the muscle

{{c2::Antinuclear antibodies::A}}

{{c2::Neurologic disorder (seizures, psychosis)::N (+2 examples)}}

mss-b7a07a05835163fea456.text: {{c1::Anticardiolipin}} is an antiphospholipid antibody that may result in false-positive {{c2::VDRL}} and {{c2::RPR}} tests
mss-b7a07a05835163fea456.extra:
- False positive syphilis test

- Venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL); rapid plasma reagin (RPR)

- Antibodies against the phospholipid β2-glycoprotein complex also bind to cardiolipin antigen, used in syphilis serology (VDRL/RPR); therefore, lupus patients may have a false positive test result for syphilis

- vs. lupus anticoagulant which results in a falsely elevated PTT

mss-3831125c3cc8be3aa7b5.text: {{c2::Lupus anticoagulant}} is an antiphospholipid antibody that results in a falsely {{c1::elevated}} {{c3::PTT}}
mss-3831125c3cc8be3aa7b5.extra:
- Because these antibodies bind to phospholipids, they may prolong the PTT (an in vitro clotting test that requires phospholipids)

- PTT will not correct when mixed with normal plasma (mixing study); prolonged PTT is an in vitro artifact

- "Falsely" elevated because patients are in a hypercoagulable, NOT hypocoagulable state

- LuPus anTicoagulanT falsely elevates PTT

- vs. anticardiolipin which is an antiphospholipid antibody that results in false positive VDRL and RPR tests

mss-a2271cc8f7af61f07476.text: Sjögren syndrome classically presents with {{c1::dry eyes}}, known as keratoconjunctivitis sicca
mss-a2271cc8f7af61f07476.extra:
- Decreased tear production and subsequent corneal damage

- Can progress to corneal ulceration

- Treatment for isolated sicca symptoms (dry eyes/mouth) consists of pilocarpine/cevimeline (M3 agonists) to increase secretions

- Steroids and DMARDs are reserved for those with extraglandular manifestations (e.g., rash, arthritis)

mss-edf1b7d3c6a02d5afb2b.text:
{{c1::Limited scleroderma}} is also referred to as "CREST syndrome":

{{c1::Calcinosis cutis::C}} (and {{c1::anti-Centromere::C}} Abs)
{{c1::Raynaud phenomenon::R}}
{{c1::Esophageal dysmotility::E}}
{{c1::Sclerodactyly (thick, tight skin)::S}}
{{c1::Telangiectasias::T}}
mss-edf1b7d3c6a02d5afb2b.extra:
Clinical features of limited scleroderma
Calcinosis
- Occurs in the subcutaneous tissue of the elbows, knees, and/or fingers
- Can break skin and leak chalky white liquid
- X-ray of the hands may show soft-tissue calcifications
Raynaud syndromeMay lead to digital ulceration / critical ischemia
Esophageal dysmotility
- Is caused by collagen deposition in the esophagus, causing atrophy of the smooth muscle
- This leads to LES hypotonia (incompetent LES)
- Leads to acid reflux and dysphagia → stricture, Barrett esophagus, and/or aspiration
Sclerodactyly
- Is fibrosis of the skin of the hands (fingers are puffy, hard to bend)
- Skin is thickened (can't pinch); becomes shiny and loses wrinkles
- Once it gets severe, patients have hands like claws
Telangiectasias
- Are skin lesions that result from dilated capillaries
- They present on the face, hands, and mucous membranes (inside the mouth)
- Women tend to have it more on the face

Calcinosis Cutis:

Photo credit: Mohammad2018, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (1st image); Image(s) licensed by DermNet and used with permission, CC-BY-NC-ND 3.0 NZ)

Raynaud:

mss-cb6dbead94e4c4e219c4.text: {{c2::Osteopetrosis}} is caused by an inherited defect in bone {{c1::resorption}}
mss-cb6dbead94e4c4e219c4.extra:
- Caused by defective osteoclasts that result in thick, dense bones without elasticity that fracture easily

- Typically presents early in life with fractures, deformities, and hematological cytopenias

mss-c5b581a9955feca78077.text: Osteopetrosis is due to poor osteo{{c1::clast}} function, impairing the ability to {{c2::remodel}} bone
mss-c5b581a9955feca78077.extra:
- Can be due to mutations in carbonic anhydrase II (required for production of H+ for the resorption pit)

- Bone remodeling strengthens and repairs bone through the removal of old bone by osteoclasts and replacement with new bone by osteoblasts

- Osteoclasts unable to generate an acidic environment → unable to dissolve hydroxyapatite → unable to resorb bone

mss-8804f184407140b926a6.text:
What are the top two causes of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease patients?

{{c1::Salmonella}} (most common) and {{c1::S. aureus}}
mss-8804f184407140b926a6.extra:
- Autosplenectomy increases the risk of salmonella infection (due to the spleen being the main defense against encapsulated organisms)

- Antibiotic coverage for Staph and Salmonella (vancomycin/clindamycin + ceftriaxone)

- Additionally, sickling in the intestinal vasculature leads to areas of necrosis, with the potential for transient mucosal breakdown and bacterial seeding in patients with sickle cell disease who may have subclinical or undiagnosed salmonella infection

mss-3ff43d9586f70fa58836.text:
The causes of {{c1::osteonecrosis}} may be remembered with the mnemonic "CASTS Bend LeGS":

{{c1::Corticosteroids::C}}
{{c1::Alcohol use disorder::A}}
{{c1::Sickle cell disease::S}}
{{c1::Trauma::T}} (most common)
{{c1::SLE::S}}

{{c1::"The Bends" (caisson disease / decompression sickness)::Bend}}

{{c1::Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease::Le}}
{{c1::Gaucher disease::G}}
{{c1::Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)::S}}
mss-3ff43d9586f70fa58836.extra:
- This card recently was updated to include lupus in the mnemonic by adding an 'S' to CAST (Dec 2024)

- Other causes include vasculitis (e.g., lupus vasculitis), bisphosphonates, and denosumab

- Corticosteroids suppress osteoblast function and stimulate osteoclast function

- Sickle cell disease can cause clots in the medial femoral circumflex artery (MCFA)

- Trauma to femoral neck (e.g., fracture) can cut off blood supply

- Bends - when diving more gas is forced into liquid due to Henry's law, on slow ascent inert gas (nitrogen) comes out of solution via "offgassing" in the lungs; rapid ascent causes offgassing to occur in the blood, resulting in gas emboli that can affect the vasculature and tissues

- Legg-Calvé-Perthes - young children 5-10; initially painless limp but with gradual onset of hip pain (no knee pain) due to ligamentum teres femoris constricting before the MCFA has time to take over the blood supply

- SCFE - obese children 11-12; knee and hip pain; increased axial force on the femoral head results in the epiphysis displacing relative to the femoral neck

mss-6470e6e509f1d5d5f6f1.text:
Which joint pathology is caused by synovitis leading to formation of a pannus (inflamed granulation tissue)?

{{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis}}
mss-6470e6e509f1d5d5f6f1.extra:
- Pannus formation leads to the erosion of cartilage and bone

- Pannus: a mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibroblasts that grows over the articular cartilage and causes erosion. Basically, it is an abnormal layer of fibrovascular tissue or granulation tissue.

- Common sites for pannus formation include over the cornea, over a joint surface (as seen in rheumatoid arthritis), or on a prosthetic heart valve

- Pannus (P) proliferates and releases cks (e.g., ILs, TNF) that eventually destroy the articular cartilage, leading to fusion of the joint by scar tissue (called ankylosis). Bone erosions are caused by osteoclasts

mss-9d763d4a776f06320d1e.extra:
Two distinct clinical presentations of gonococcal arthritis are possible:

Arthritis-dermatitis syndrome:
- Polyarthralgias: migratory, asymmetric arthritis that may become purulent
- Tenosynovitis: simultaneous inflammation of several tendons (e.g., fingers, toes, wrist, ankle)
- Dermatitis: vesicular, pustular, or maculopapular lesions

Purulent gonococcal arthritis:
- Abrupt inflammation in up to 4 joints (commonly knees, ankles, and wrists)
- No skin manifestations
- Rarely tenosynovitis

mss-e5d8b3f8cda378e6dfd2.text:
What glycogen storage disorder is a cause of secondary gout?

{{c1::Von Gierke disease}}
mss-e5d8b3f8cda378e6dfd2.extra:
- Deficiency in glucose-6-phosphatase → failure of the Cori cycle → build-up of lactate in the blood

- Lactate is an organic anion, and is a counterion for uric acid at the URAT1 antiporter on the apical surface of the collecting duct; thus, the more lactate secreted into the urine, more uric acid reabsorbed into the blood




Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

mss-698d27c1dd44948a9ca7.text: {{c2::Myasthenia gravis}} is caused by autoantibodies to {{c1::post}}synaptic {{c1::ACh receptors}} at the NMJ
mss-698d27c1dd44948a9ca7.extra:
- Importantly, these antibodies (IgM and/or IgG) block activation resulting in a reduced number of functional acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction

- This results in a decreased end plate potential (not allowing muscle cells to depolarize) since there are fewer postsynaptic cation channels that can now open in response to acetylcholine

mss-215d35f87df726ce143a.text: Myasthenia gravis presents with muscle weakness that {{c1::worsens}} with muscle use
mss-215d35f87df726ce143a.extra:
- AKA muscle fatigability

- When a motor nerve releases its neurotransmitters, it needs time to reuptake acetylcholine from synaptic cleft

- However given frequent, repeated contractions, not enough time for acetylcholine to be replenished in axon terminal, and the amount of acetylcholine released gets smaller and smaller

- In a normal person, it would take exercise for this to manifest, however in a person with MG, they are dealing with a decreased amount of motor end plate receptors so this manifests with normal activity (less sites to bind and cause muscle contraction), resulting in a decreased end plate potential

mss-73eba75b81d9ef30c161.text: Acne vulgaris is due to chronic inflammation of hair follicles and associated {{c1::sebaceous}} glands, which secrete their contents through a(n) {{c1::holocrine}} mechanism
mss-73eba75b81d9ef30c161.extra:
- May result in comedones (white heads, black heads), pustules (pimples), or nodules (scarring)
[Holy, that’s a lot of Sebum!]
[DHT increases sebum secretion]

- Hair follicle keratinization with keratin plug formation
- Sebaceous gland hypertrophy with increased sebum production
- The gland is colonized with cutibacterium acnes (formerly propionibacterium acnes)
- Hydrolysis of TAGs in sebum by bacteria and inflammatory fatty acids production


Photo credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC)
Angiosarcoma of the liver
Lung cancer
mss-96e41b6fe935bc089f8c.extra:
- Arsenic likes to bind to cysteine residues in keratin (explaining predilection for causing SCC of the skin), thus the presence of this compound can be detected by sampling a patients fingernails or hair

*Memory Key: long ago working women would apply arsenic to the skin so it would lighten and they wouldn't look tan

CarcinogenAssociated CancerKey Details
AflatoxinsHepatocellular carcinomaFrom Aspergillus (contaminates stored grains)
Alkylating agentsLeukemia, lymphomaChemotherapy side effect
AlcoholOropharyngeal and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma
ArsenicSkin squamous cell carcinoma, lung cancer, liver angiosarcomaFound in cigarette smoke
AsbestosLung carcinoma, mesotheliomaMore likely to cause lung cancer than mesothelioma
Cigarette smokeOropharyngeal, esophageal, lung, kidney, bladder, pancreatic carcinomaMajor global carcinogen; polycyclic hydrocarbons are key culprits
NitrosaminesStomach carcinomaLinked to smoked foods (high rates in Japan)
NaphthylamineBladder urothelial carcinomaFound in cigarette smoke
Vinyl chlorideLiver angiosarcomaOccupational hazard (used in PVC production)
Nickel, chromium, beryllium, silicaLung carcinomaOccupational hazard

mss-aabb7bef0a271bcf881d.text: In {{c1::endochondral}} ossification, osteoblasts and osteoclasts replace cartilage with a matrix of {{c2::woven}} bone and then remodel to {{c3::lamellar}} bone
mss-aabb7bef0a271bcf881d.extra:
- This occurs at the diaphysis (primary center ossification) and the epiphyses (secondary centers of ossification).

- Blasts = Build Bone
- Clasts = Crush (resorb)

- Woven = random fiber orientation
- Lamellar = parallel fibers arranged in layers (each layer is perpendicular to the adjacent lamellae)

What is the likely diagnosis in a patient with a facial rash that worsens with sun exposure, and a history of DVT, transient ischemic attacks, and two miscarriages?

mss-43aeeaf6ab0619195c1b.extra:

- Antibodies react with platelets activating endothelial cells / platelets → thrombosis

{{c1::High-dose glucocorticoids}}

mss-02ac93d590c3874f53f8.text:
What is the likely diagnosis in a patient who recently finished taking penicillin that presents with mild fever, myalgias or arthralgias, and painful violaceous rash?

{{c1::Hypersensitivity vasculitis (cutaneous small vessel vasculitis)}}
mss-02ac93d590c3874f53f8.extra:
Photo credit: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

- This is a leukocytoclastic vasculitis (type III HSR) involving post-capillary venules in the dermis

- Usually seen with infections (HCV, HIV) or medications (penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides, allpurionol, PTU, phenytoin)

- Dark red spots are palpable purpura (spots are non-blanching)

- Biopsy shows perivascular neutrophils and neutrophilic nuclear debris ("leukocytoclasia")


Photo credit: Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Libre Pathology

mss-0309572665b0b6982c89.text: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) results from inflammation of the {{c1::gluteus medius}} or {{c1::minimus}} tendons located lateral to the greater trochanter of the femur
mss-0309572665b0b6982c89.extra:
- Typically due to gluteus medius overuse / tendinitis

- Previously known as trochanteric bursitis, renamed as bursa involvement is uncommon

- Initial treatment includes local heat, activity modification and NSAIDs; PT often helpful; treat persistent symptoms with corticosteroid injection

mss-d0ff49dea6f9c39e823b.extra:
- Previously known as trochanteric bursitis, renamed as bursa involvement is uncommon

- Gluteus medius tendon rubs against the trochanteric bursa, causing the tendon to become inflamed

- Often seen in patients who run on banked surfaces; can be due to instability from a labral tear or ligament injury

mss-cfbfe95817f3425f575f.text: Abnormal prenatal development of the <u>acetabulum</u> is caused by excessive {{c1::uterine packing (uterine constraint)}}

Which of the following usually occurs in children between 10-16 years old?

mss-72ef47453a86b38517bb.extra:

- The resultant change in vasculature manifests with a suboptimal blood supply to the growth plate → unstable growth plate which can be sheared by axial force

mss-c12a94c3c5c0fbb7b08a.text: In Legg-Calvé-Perthes, there is a(n) {{c1::idiopathic}} mechanism of obstruction of blood to the femoral head
mss-c12a94c3c5c0fbb7b08a.extra:
- Thought to be related to factors that disrupt blood supply to the femoral head (coagulation abnormalities, trauma)

- If blood supply to the epiphysis is disrupted, the bone dies → avascular necrosis


Photo credit: Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Disrupted articular cartilage with underneath irregular necrotic and collapsed yellow dead bone:

Photo credit: © Dr. Jian-Hua Qiao, all rights reserved, via Flickr (used with permission)

mss-6b97f90d1442781b6c55.text: In slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), increased {{c1::axial}} force on the femoral head results in the femoral {{c2::epiphysis}} displacing relative to femoral neck
mss-6b97f90d1442781b6c55.extra:
- Thus obese children have an increased axial force (due to their weight) applied to an unstable growth plate; slippage impacts MCFA

- On imaging, this looks like a scoop of ice cream slipping off of a cone

Photo credit: Baig et al., CC BY 3.0, via Cureus

mss-5d31cd3e98e5c155cebb.text:
In Legg-Calvé-Perthes, will you often observe pathology on the initial x-ray?

{{c1::No}}
mss-5d31cd3e98e5c155cebb.extra:
- Plain radiographic changes are delayed 6 weeks or more from clinical onset, and since clinical symptoms will elicit the initial x-ray being taken, these are usually not seen

- However, a distinguishing feature from a SCFE is that LCP patients will have increased width of the femoral neck


Photo credit: Hellerhoff, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

LCP disease of the right hip
Photo credit: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mss-3e9a04284ca3a9b13158.text:
What procedure is both diagnostic and therapeutic for septic arthritis?

{{c1::Arthrocentesis (to drain synovial fluid)}}
mss-3e9a04284ca3a9b13158.extra:
- Arthrocentesis: a diagnostic and/or therapeutic procedure in which synovial fluid from a joint is aspirated using a sterile needle to determine the etiology of joint effusions, as well as to relieve pain or pressure from a joint

- Should be performed prior to empiric antibiotic therapy to minimize false negative results

mss-299ce5aa24d2e5b68a32.text:
What maneuvers are both diagnostic and therapeutic for radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow)?

{{c1::Forearm hyperpronation
OR
supination plus flexion::2}}
mss-299ce5aa24d2e5b68a32.extra:
- Hyperpronation maneuver: Hyperpronate the forearm (with the elbow extended or flexed at 90 degrees)

- Supination-flexion maneuver: Supinate the forearm, then immediately flex the elbow

- Does not need post-reduction films because successful reduction of radial head subluxation is both diagnostic and therapeutic

mss-520564330a63ca87f331.text:
What is the likely diagnosis in a child that presents with two months of daily fever, pink macular rash, and knee / hip pain that is worse in the morning?

mss-520564330a63ca87f331.extra:
- Systemic type JIA is also known as Still disease; most common in patients 2 – 4 years old

- Symptoms: salmon-pink macular rash, hepatosplenomegaly, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, myalgias, fever, joint swelling and pain, pericarditis, pleuritis, myocarditis

- Lab findings: leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia, and elevated ESR

Salmon colored macular rash (left); Destructive changes in the hips (right)

Photo credit: Giancane et al.,(2016) IL-1 Inhibition in Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis. Front. Pharmacol. 7:467. doi: 10.3389/fphar.2016.00467. CC BY 4.0, modified by cropping

mss-94e3640c66459e7e9d67.text: Prostate metastases have a high predilection for the spine due to the connection of the prostate to the {{c1::Batson}} venous plexus
mss-94e3640c66459e7e9d67.extra:
- The Batson venous plexus is a valveless venous network connecting the deep pelvic veins (draining the bladder, prostate, and rectum) to the internal vertebral venous plexus in the epidural space

- It also communicates with the brain’s venous system through connections with the dural venous sinuses, enabling bidirectional blood flow. This unique anatomy plays a role in intracranial pressure regulation

Photo credit: G. Elhammady, A. Schubeck, V. El-Najjar, M. Robinson, "Postmortem Demonstration of the Source of Pulmonary Thromboembolism: The Importance of the Autopsy", Case Reports in Vascular Medicine. CC BY

DRESS syndrome
Drug Allopurinol and antiepileptics (e.g., phenytoin, carbamazepine)
Reaction (rash) Morbilliform starting on the face/upper trunk → becomes widespread
Facial edema is common
Eosinophilia ↑ eosinophil count
Systemic symptoms Fever/malaise
Diffuse lymphadenopathy
~90% of patients have involvement of ≥1 organ system (e.g., liver [transaminitis], kidney, lung)

mss-69b22a83bbcc0e58d6ff.text:
How do the following laboratory values change in secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease (CKD)?

PTH: {{c1::Increased}}
Ca2+: {{c1::Decreased}}
Phosphorus: {{c1::Increased}}
mss-69b22a83bbcc0e58d6ff.extra:
- Can't pee out phosphate, which ends up binding with Ca2+

- Secondary hyperparathyroidism is usually an adaptive response to prolonged hypocalcemia caused by either chronic kidney disease or vitamin D deficiency

- This condition results in parathyroid hyperplasia and excessive secretion of PTH, even though serum calcium levels may be low or normal

- Although uncommon, the condition may require surgical intervention, affecting only 1% of the US dialysis population each year

mss-df00936327f40545be7c.text: Deep venous thrombosis is treated with {{c1::anticoagulants}} to prevent thrombus propagation, {{c1::thrombolytics}} to bust the clot, and a(n) {{c1::IVC filter}} for treatment-refractory patients
mss-df00936327f40545be7c.extra:
- Anticoagulants: heparin → warfarin
- Thrombolytics: tPA or streptokinase
- IVC filter only prevents PE, not DVT

Management:
- IV heparin or subcutaneous LMWH
- Submassive PE: consider tPA
- Massive PE: tPA vs. pulmonary embolectomy
- IVC filter: only if contraindication to anticoagulation

- In cases where there is a strong suspicion of VTE (venous thromboembolism) administer heparin immediately, even before the diagnosis is confirmed then a CT angiogram of the pulmonary arteries should be obtained

mss-7c1d6f900ed593ebcd1b.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease caused by {{c1::complement}}-forming complexes; it more often affects {{c1::women::gender}} and {{c1::people of color::ethnicity}}
mss-7c1d6f900ed593ebcd1b.extra:
Criteria for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
ClinicalImmunologic
• Acute cutaneous lupus
• Chronic cutaneous lupus
• Oral or nasal ulcers
• Non-scarring alopecia
• Arthritis
• Serositis
• Renal
• Neurologic
• Hemolytic anemia
• Leukopenia
• Thrombocytopenia (< 100,000/mm3)		• ANA
• Anti-DNA
• Anti-Smith
• Antiphospholipid Ab
• Low complement (C3,C4, CHSO)
• Direct Coombs
4 criteria required, with at least 1 clinical and 1 laboratory OR biopsy-proven lupus nephritis with positive ANA or Anti-DNA

mss-ba46b368fba64ea18584.text:
Can distal symptoms occur in polymyalgia rheumatica?

{{c1::Yes}}
mss-ba46b368fba64ea18584.extra:
- Symptoms of PMR include pain and stiffness in the upper arms, limited shoulder movement, pelvic girdle pain, and lumbar region pain. Initially, the symptoms can be unilateral but soon become symmetrical

- In about half of patients, mild distal symptoms accompany the characteristic proximal pain and stiffness. These distal symptoms are commonly observed at the wrists and MCP joints, and sometimes at the knees but not the feet and ankles. Carpal tunnel syndromes can also be found in some patients. Explosive symptoms at the hands and wrists are rare

- "Blast is bright"

mss-d7bb3dcd9d17a812c6b4.text:
Is weight loss or exercise more important to reduce risk of osteoarthritis?

{{c1::Weight loss}}
mss-d7bb3dcd9d17a812c6b4.extra:
- Reduce burden on the knees

- Distinguish the risk factors for osteoarthritis vs. treatment (which includes exercise)

- Vigorous exercise can actually INCREASE the risk for osteoarthritis

- Risk factors: advanced age (> 50 years), obesity, female sex, joint trauma, genetics, anatomic factors, lifestyle factors

- Treatments: supportive measures (heat, decreased weight-bearing exercises, use of cane/crutches), NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroid injections, hyaluronate injections, joint replacement

Are nonpharmacologic treatments or pharmacological treatments used first in treatment of osteoarthritis?

{{c1::Non-pharmacologic}}

- Lifestyle changes: weight management, exercises, decrease weight-bearing exercises
- Braces, foot orthoses, cane, crutches
- Heat

- Oral and topical NSAIDs
- Topical capsaicin
- Duloxetine
- Intraarticular glucocorticoid injections
- Hyaluronate injections for viscosupplementation

Surgical treatment: joint replacement

mss-9fe6355be18ab97bc58f.text: Advanced rheumatoid arthritis may cause {{c1::fibrous ankylosis}} (near-fused joints) and {{c1::pannus}} (fibrovascular synovial hyperplasia)
mss-9fe6355be18ab97bc58f.extra:
- Pannus: a mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibroblasts that grows over the articular cartilage and causes erosion. Basically, it is an abnormal layer of fibrovascular tissue or granulation tissue.

- Common sites for pannus formation include over the cornea, over a joint surface (as seen in rheumatoid arthritis), or on a prosthetic heart valve.

- Pannus (P) proliferates and releases cks (e.g., ILs, TNF) that eventually destroy the articular cartilage, leading to fusion of the joint by scar tissue (called ankylosis). Bone erosions are caused by osteoclasts.

mss-90420de0657cd41452bb.text: {{c1::Type II (senile)}} osteoporosis is characterized by normal osteoclast activity with decreased osteoblast activity
mss-90420de0657cd41452bb.extra:
- This is termed a “low-turnover” osteoporosis precisely because osteoclast activity is normal

- With age, osteoblasts lose their ability to proliferate and form bone. However, osteoclast activity is not affected by the aging process. Thus, after reaching peak bone mass around age 30, decreased osteoblast activity with normal osteoclast activity will result in an overall decrease in bone density (average 0.7% / year)

mss-3c5a7b08f3adcb8d85cc.text: A positive patellar grind test (Clarke test) is pain upon {{c1::isometric contraction of the quadriceps}} and is suggestive of patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS)
mss-3c5a7b08f3adcb8d85cc.extra:
- Positive test is indicative of any patellofemoral joint disorders (i.e., patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS), chondromalacia patellae, and patellofemoral osteoarthritis)

- Patellar grind test: performed with the patient supine and the knee extended. The examiner applies downward pressure superior to the patella while the patient contracts the quadriceps

- Patellar compression test: performed by applying downward pressure directly to the patella while the patient contracts the quadriceps

mss-bd9f1f41dce8e5d9a397.text: Chronic gout may lead to formation of a(n) {{c1::pannus}}, which is a layer of granulation tissue inside the joint capsule due to ongoing inflammation
mss-bd9f1f41dce8e5d9a397.extra:
- Pannus: a mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibroblasts that grows over the articular cartilage and causes erosion. Basically, it is an abnormal layer of fibrovascular tissue or granulation tissue.

- Common sites for pannus formation include over the cornea, over a joint surface (as seen in rheumatoid arthritis), or on a prosthetic heart valve.

- Pannus (P) proliferates and releases cks (e.g., ILs, TNF) that eventually destroy the articular cartilage, leading to fusion of the joint by scar tissue (called ankylosis). Bone erosions are caused by osteoclasts.

- Type I cryoglobulinemia: an immune-mediated disorder characterized by the deposition of monoclonal immunoglobulins (IgG and IgM) within blood vessels; most commonly associated with protein-secreting monoclonal gammopathies, including monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, and multiple myeloma

- Type II (mixed) cryoglobulins are monoclonal IgM and polyclonal IgG antibodies

- Type III (mixed) cryoglobulins are polyclonal IgM and polyclonal IgG antibodies

Causes of {{c1::drug-induced lupus (DILE)}} may be remembered with the mnemonic "HEαPS PIMP":

{{c1::Hydralazine::H}}
{{c1::Etanercept::E}}
{{c1::α-methyldopa / IFN-α::α (2)}}
{{c1::Phenytoin::P}}
{{c1::Sulfa drugs::S}}

{{c1::Procainamide::P}}
{{c1::Isoniazid::I}}
{{c1::Methimazole::M}}
{{c1::Propylthiouracil (PTU)::P}}
mss-3e731afa5b1bfde934dd.extra:
- Associated with anti-histone antibodies

- Underlying etiology is believed to be genetic (presence of a genetic mutation that causes decreased acetyltransferase activity or presence of HLA-DR2, HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, or an unexpressed C4 complement allele)

- Also minocycline

mss-29abb8699d7691d33729.text: {{c1::Waardenburg}} syndrome presents with patchy depigmentation of the skin, hair, and irises; sometimes associated with deafness
mss-29abb8699d7691d33729.extra:
- Patients typically present with a white forelock and eyelashes, iridic heterochromia, depigmented skin patches, limb abnormalities, facial abnormalities (broad nasal root, cleft lip or palate), and sensorineural hearing loss

- Due to defect in differentiation of neural crest cells into melanocytes

- Ten disease subtypes caused by a variety of genetic mutations; most common are PAX3 and SOX10


Photo credit: Mohammad2018, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
